Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Eighteen months ago, Nisha had been on a commercial retrofit job when a corroded valve she had been tightening finally sheared under torque. A pressurized line of industrial degreaser and solvent mist erupted across the narrow crawlspace, coating her face, hair, and lungs in a thick, acrid cloud. She remembered the immediate, suffocating burn in her throat, the way her vision blurred, and the frantic, breathless scramble to tear off her gloves and drag herself toward the stairwell. She had come to believe that if she had stayed even a minute longer, the fumes would have sealed her airway for good. In the weeks that followed, the physical toll of the exposure settled into a permanent tightness in her chest and a lingering metallic taste that no amount of brushing could erase. The crawlspace became the architecture of her days. As a plumber, Nisha spent her hours crawling beneath floors and peering into utility shafts, but her work was no longer just about wrenches and pipe fittings. She had learned to treat any unfamiliar scent as a potential rupture of that same invisible barrier she felt had failed her. During a routine basement service call, a neighbor’s overloaded electrical outlet sparked and released a sharp, acrid whiff of overheated plastic. Nisha’s breath hitched instantly. Her heart hammered against her ribs, a violent, familiar thrumming that made her hands tremble so badly she could barely hold her multimeter. She had to drop her tools, press her palms against the concrete floor, and wait through the wave of dizziness until the sensation passed. What frightened her most was how instantly her body had remembered the chemical. The watchfulness stood alongside her daily life as a quiet, relentless routine. She would never sit with her back to a door, her eyes constantly tracing ceiling corners for smoke detectors, scanning floor grates, and watching neighboring windows for stray smoke. She kept her car keys in her pocket, certain that an emergency would require a sudden exit. Medical care, however, was strictly off-limits. Every time her husband suggested a routine physical examination or mentioned an ambulance in a television drama, a cold dread would pool in her stomach. She had come to believe that hospitals were places where bodies were stripped of control, where the very air smelled of failure and sterile chemicals. She simply stopped going, trusting instead in the quiet certainty that staying away was the only way to stay safe. The constant on-guard posture accompanied her evenings and her marriage. Nisha found herself steering every conversation toward logistics—scheduling, errands, the mechanics of the day—carefully sidestepping anything that might stir up negative or positive feelings. She had come to believe that any strong emotional shift was a vulnerability she could not afford. Her nights offered no respite. She would drift into sleep only to jolt awake around two in the morning, convinced she was still breathing in fumes. She would rise quietly, pace the hallway, and press her fingers to her own wrist, waking alert to check whether she was safe until she was convinced the house was secure. By morning, the exhaustion left her shoulders tight and her thoughts fragmented, but the ritual kept the panic at bay. The breaking point arrived not with a panic attack, but with a quiet accumulation. After the electrical spark incident, Nisha found herself unable to open her tool cabinets for three days, the rubber hose linings triggering a fresh wave of nausea. Her husband noticed how she flinched at the burnt smell of his morning cooking, how she had stopped laughing at his jokes, and how she now slept with one eye open. He left a clinic referral on the kitchen counter, and for the first time, the weight of carrying it all alone felt heavier than the fear itself. She had come to the office that week not because she wanted to relive the crawlspace, but because she was tired of waking up in a safe house, convinced she was still drowning, and desperate to find a way to simply breathe again.
